title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the 

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.




There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.




Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.

author: WoMin
title: Revisiting Ubuntu for our collective liberation
content:
Reflecting on the Afrocentric International Feminist Organising School




From 11 to 15 September 2026, the 

Berta Caceres International Feminist Organising School (IFOS)

 convened in Nairobi, Kenya. Co-organised by the Grassroots Global Justice Alliance, the Indigenous Environmental Network, and the World March of Women, it brought together over 150 participants from 37 countries and territories. Grounded in a decolonial and Pan African vision, the programme created space to explore interconnected struggles and alternatives. Discussions centred on climate justice, agroecology, land rights, sovereignty, and the Nature Commons.




Ubuntu revisited




One of the running themes of the school was the philosophy of Ubuntu. Rooted in Southern African ways of life, Ubuntu is a living tradition that shapes how we relate to one another and to the world around us, both physical and spiritual. Ubuntu invites us to recognise one another’s personhood and our interdependence as part of the broader web of Life.







“Ubuntu is

 

often introduced through the phrase ‘umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’, commonly translated as ‘a person is a person through other people’ or simply

 

‘I am because we are’. Ubuntu calls us to see

 

personhood as fundamentally relational.

 

With Xenophobia and Afrophobia on the continent in service of right-wing agenda, we must reclaim Ubuntu.”-

 

Khwezilomso

author: WoMin
title: Press Release | African Women Leading the Fight for Climate Justice
content:
From 5–8 October 2026, Yaoundé, Cameroon, will host the fourth regional 

Women’s Climate Assembly

 (WCA) under the theme 

Our lands, our voices: African women united for climate justice and reparations

! The landmark gathering unites women across West and Central Africa to strengthen their fight for climate justice rooted in ecofeminist resistance and the defence of the commons—land, forests, water, seeds and other resources collectively sustained and stewarded by communities. While Africa’s contribution to global greenhouse gas emissions remains minimal, its communities—particularly women in rural, coastal, and forest areas—face disproportionate climate impacts. The WCA highlights this fundamental injustice and the climate debt owed by historically polluting nations and multinationals to the continent.




The overall objective of the Women’s Climate Assembly is to strengthen and unify a Pan African ecofeminist movement for climate justice that connects women’s collective struggles. Key objectives include women’s leadership, fostering shared strategies for climate justice, promoting community-based alternatives centred on food sovereignty and sustainable resource management, and advancing calls for climate reparations and just development models.
